questions.q: You convert sales from ₹ lakh to rupees (multiply by 1,00,000) before computing their correlation with ad spend. What happens to Pearson's r?
options: It is multiplied by 1,00,000
It does not change
It is divided by 1,00,000
It becomes 1
questions.why: Correlation divides the covariance by both standard deviations, so the unit change cancels out. The **covariance** is multiplied by 1,00,000, which is exactly why correlation, not covariance, is used to describe strength.

questions.q: Ad spend and sales have r = 0.6. What share of the variation in sales does a straight-line fit on ad spend account for?
questions.why: r² = 0.6² = 0.36, so 36%. Reading r itself as a percentage (60%) overstates the fit; 77% is √0.6, which goes the wrong way.

questions.q: Ice-cream sales and drownings are positively correlated. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A confounder: hot weather increases both swimming and ice-cream sales
Drownings cause people to buy ice cream
Eating ice cream causes drowning
The correlation must be a calculation error
questions.why: A confounder influences both variables and creates a correlation even though neither causes the other. Correlation alone cannot tell you the direction or existence of a causal link.

questions.q: Two variables have covariance 12, with standard deviations 3 and 5. What is Pearson's r?
questions.why: r = covariance ÷ (s_x × s_y) = 12 / (3 × 5) = 0.80. 2.40 divides by only one SD, and 4.00 = 12 / 3 likewise; any "correlation" outside −1 to +1 signals a mistake. 0.64 is r².

questions.q: Across eight stores, footfall and sales give Pearson r = 0.06 but Spearman ρ = 0.33. Earlier data showed r ≈ 0.99. What should you suspect first?
options: The relationship has genuinely disappeared
Spearman is always lower than Pearson
An outlier or data-entry error is distorting Pearson's r; plot the data and check the records
The sample is too large
questions.why: A single wrong value (sales typed as 5 instead of 45) can wipe out Pearson's r, while Spearman, using ranks, is hurt far less. A big gap between the two is a warning sign. Always look at the scatter plot before concluding anything.

questions.q: When is Spearman's rank correlation a better choice than Pearson's r?
options: When the relationship is a perfectly straight line with no outliers
When both variables are categorical labels such as city names
When you want to measure a U-shaped relationship
When the relationship is consistently rising or falling but curved, when there are outliers, or when the data are ranks or 1–5 ratings
questions.why: Spearman measures monotonic relationships and resists outliers. For a clean straight line Pearson is fine. A U-shape is not monotonic, so Spearman misses it too, and unordered labels such as city names have no ranks.

questions.q: With 10,000 customers, the correlation between age and basket size is r = 0.03 with p = 0.003. How should you report it?
options: Statistically significant but negligible: r² = 0.0009, so age explains less than 0.1% of the variation in basket size
A strong relationship, because p is far below 0.05
Not significant, because r is close to zero
Proof that age causes larger baskets
questions.why: With large samples even tiny correlations are significant. Look at r and r², not just the p-value. Significance concerns whether r is exactly zero, which is a different question from importance, and observational correlation never proves causation.

questions.q: In an interview: "Twelve months of data show r = 0.85 between ad spend and sales, but the budget rises every festival season. How would you find out whether ads drive sales?"
options: The correlation is high, so ads clearly drive sales
Compute Spearman as well; if it is also high, causation is proven
Recognise season as a confounder and run a randomised experiment, such as a geo-experiment that varies spend across regions; if that is impossible, use causal methods and state the assumptions
Remove the festival months and recompute r
questions.why: Randomisation is the gold standard for causation because it breaks the link with confounders like season. A second correlation measure has the same problem. Dropping months just throws away data and may leave other confounders in place.
